tagline: Cinder cones and basalt flows on a bumpy volcanic loop.
intro: Lunar Crater Back Country Byway is a 24-mile loop through a volcanic field of cinder cones and basalt flows. The road is unpaved and bumpy; the Bureau of Land Management allows one to two hours for the drive. BLM lists it as a Type II Back Country Byway and highlights the volcanic formations along the route. Easy Chair Crater appears early, with Lunar Crater farther along. The wider volcanic field extends along the Reveille and Pancake Ranges in Nye County, central Nevada.

The landscape’s varied geology and accessibility made it a training ground for Moon-bound astronauts and a testing ground for prototype Mars rovers. In 1973 the volcanic field received National Natural Landmark designation. The field contains more than 200 vents, including small volcanic cones, lava flows and explosion craters called maars. Lunar Crater itself is one of those maars.

From Tonopah, take US 6 east toward Ely to approximately mile marker 79, where a sign marks the loop on the right. A parking place lies at the foot of Easy Chair Crater. Continue through the rock formations to Lunar Crater, where the loop provides a stopping point for viewing the crater. From Lunar Crater, BLM describes a view of 20 other volcanoes nearby.

moments.title: Easy Chair Crater
moments.text: Easy Chair is one of the first craters visible on the byway, with a parking place at its foot. The feature is a ridge in the Lunar Lake basin, about 790 feet high and approximately 1.6 miles long. Volcanic fragments accumulated along a fissure vent to form the ridge. Two scoria cones and a maar partly buried or destroyed it; the cones also supplied a field of lava flows. In this volcanic field, maars formed where rising magma met groundwater, while cones grew where material thrown from vents piled up.

moments.title: Lunar Crater
moments.text: Lunar Crater is almost circular, with a rim of volcanic material enclosing a hollow 3,600 feet wide and 430 feet deep. It cuts into basaltic lava, underlying tuff and two older volcanic cones. The bottom holds an alluvial fan and a playa, at the lowest point in the volcanic field. Its exact age is not known. The byway passes a stopping point where visitors can get out to view the crater, and a parking place lies on the rim. Around the margins lie beds of volcanic material, including ash, scoria and blocks of tuff.
moments.notice: A ring of volcanic material defines the crater’s rim.

moments.title: Volcanoes beyond the rim
moments.text: From Lunar Crater, the view includes 20 other nearby volcanoes. They belong to a field extending along the Reveille and Pancake Ranges, with more than 200 vents. Erosion has exposed the structures beneath some volcanoes and left lava-capped mesas elsewhere. The field’s activity began about six million years ago, while its most recent eruption was about 38,000 years ago. The same field’s diverse geology and accessibility made it useful for astronaut training and prototype Mars-rover tests. Volcanic activity continued over millions of years, leaving the different volcanic centers eroded to different degrees.

practical: Easy Chair Crater: BLM classifies the loop for high-clearance vehicles. Keep vehicles on existing roads and trails. (checked 2026-10-11)
